strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: KV-cache growth during long reasoning generations. Combining adaptive precision, progressive eviction, and memory-slot reuse is a potentially useful algorithm–system contribution.
Reports promising accuracy–memory trade-offs across multiple reasoning-model families and mathematics and coding benchmarks. The breadth of models is a strength.

Includes substantial component and hyperparameter ablations. Table 2’s fixed-batch comparison without quantization provides useful evidence that avoiding gather-based compaction can improve throughput independently of precision reduction.

Provides pseudocode, quantization-format descriptions, memory-layout illustrations, and operation-level profiling, and explicitly acknowledges the lack of integration with production serving frameworks.
weaknesses: The eviction policy does not explain how it satisfies the evaluated hard cache budgets. Section 3.3 requires retaining at least four tokens from every 128-token segment, implying a minimum cache that grows with generation length. At 32K generated tokens, historical segments alone require approximately 1024 tokens, making smaller evaluated budgets infeasible without an additional segment-deletion or merging rule. Neither the text nor pseudocode specifies what happens when every candidate reaches minimum retention. This materially affects the interpretation of the compression results.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution of thought awareness. Eviction baselines use full precision, whereas ThinKV also quantizes; quantization comparisons use different formats and precision levels. Missing controls include uniform quantization plus the same eviction mechanism, quantized R-KV, and periodic or randomly triggered segment annealing with identical retention schedules and clustering. Related hybrid methods such as Q-Hitter and MiniKV are discussed but not evaluated. Table 3 establishes component utility, but does not establish that semantic thought adaptation causes the gains.

The central thought-decomposition interpretation is insufficiently validated. Selected sparsity traces, illustrative keywords, and a few association maps do not demonstrate reliable identification of reasoning, execution, and transition segments across tasks. There is no quantitative agreement with independent annotations or robustness analysis after compression changes the attention distribution. Moreover, the implemented R4E4T2 configuration gives reasoning and execution identical precision, weakening the evidence that all three semantic categories are necessary.

Important algorithm details are ambiguous or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 intersects layers exhibiting exactly three modes across all calibration prompts, but does not specify how exactly four layers are selected or what happens if the intersection is empty; KDE bandwidth is also unspecified. The main text classifies using sparsity averaged over selected layers, whereas the pseudocode classifies each layer separately. K-means centroids generally are not existing keys with corresponding value tokens, yet the eviction description alternates between centroid replacement and selection of representative token pairs.

The system description leaves correctness and memory accounting unresolved. Reusing arbitrary slots in per-channel quantized key groups requires explaining how old and new tokens retain compatible scales. Likewise, permutation invariance alone does not establish that an unchanged attention kernel correctly handles partially evicted blocks, validity masks, and model-specific attention restrictions. Reported memory footprints lack a clear breakdown of scales, full-precision buffers, metadata, and unreclaimed slots.

The accuracy evaluation lacks sufficient statistical and reproducibility detail. AIME contains only 30 sampled problems, making small reported differences difficult to interpret without rollout counts, seeds, or uncertainty estimates. LiveCodeBench version and date range, decoding settings, exact checkpoint revisions, and baseline tuning are insufficiently specified. The broad 'near-lossless' claim also needs qualification: Table 1 includes a roughly five-point LiveCodeBench drop for QwQ-32B, and Table 7 reports a 7.4-point GSM8K drop.

The headline throughput gain is demonstrated on one 8B model under fixed 32K-token generation and maximum feasible batch sizes; 5.8× is against the sequential-gather implementation, while the overlapped baseline narrows the gain. The controlled comparison is valuable, but realistic variable-length serving, latency constraints, and optimized serving-engine comparisons are missing. Consequently, the evidence supports a promising prototype more strongly than the paper’s broad deployment claims.

strengths: Addresses an important inference bottleneck with a coherent combination of attention-based segmentation, mixed-precision quantization, progressive eviction, and memory-slot reuse.
The reported evaluation spans several reasoning-model families and mathematics/coding benchmarks. Figure 8 and Table 3 show promising accuracy retention under substantial compression.
The systems evaluation includes two GPU platforms, overhead breakdowns, and an equal-batch, approximately equal-compression comparison. These provide useful evidence beyond accuracy-only experiments.
weaknesses: The eviction policy does not explain how its hard budget can coexist with retaining at least four tokens from every 128-token segment. After 2,048 generated tokens, those retained tokens alone exhaust a 64-token budget; longer generations necessarily exceed it. Section 3.3 and the pseudocode provide no fallback for segments already at minimum retention. This directly affects the validity of the small-budget experiments.

The comparisons do not isolate the main contribution adequately. Eviction baselines lack quantization, while quantization baselines lack eviction. Missing controls include R-KV combined with comparable quantization, existing hybrid methods such as Q-Hitter/MiniKV, and periodic segment eviction without thought labels. Consequently, the gains cannot be confidently attributed to thought adaptation rather than combining established compression mechanisms and changing eviction frequency.

The semantic interpretation of attention sparsity is insufficiently validated. Selected traces and illustrative keywords do not establish reliable correspondence between sparsity regimes and reasoning, execution, or transition categories. There is no quantitative labeling validation or random-label control, and stability after compression changes the attention distribution is not established.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. K-means centroids are not generally existing tokens, yet the method retains their 'corresponding' values without specifying representative selection. Reusing individual slots also requires explaining how per-channel quantization scales remain associated with surviving and newly inserted keys. Permutation invariance alone does not justify unchanged attention computation with mixed precision, eviction masks, and partially reused groups.

The accuracy evaluation lacks information needed to substantiate 'near-lossless' performance: sampling settings, rollout counts, uncertainty estimates, and the LiveCodeBench version are unspecified. AIME contains only 30 problems, making small differences particularly uncertain. Some losses are material: Table 1 reports a 4.98-point LiveCodeBench drop for QwQ-32B, and Table 7 reports a 7.4-point GSM8K drop.

The headline throughput improvement is measured for one 8B model generating a fixed 32K tokens, with each method using its maximum batch size. The equal-batch experiment is helpful, but removing TBQ still leaves different eviction policies, so it does not isolate the memory-management kernel alone. Realistic serving workloads and comparisons with optimized hybrid baselines are absent; the claimed generalization to production serving engines remains untested.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the substantial appendix. Algorithm 1 does not specify KDE bandwidth, how exactly four layers are selected from the intersection, or what happens when too few qualify. The generation pseudocode classifies thoughts independently per layer, whereas the main method averages sparsity over selected layers. These discrepancies leave the implemented algorithm ambiguous.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: KV-cache growth during long reasoning outputs. Combining adaptive compression with memory-slot reuse is a relevant algorithm–system contribution.
Reports promising accuracy–memory trade-offs across multiple reasoning-model families and mathematics and coding benchmarks, with substantial improvements over several recent eviction baselines.

The system evaluation includes two GPU platforms, overhead breakdowns, and an equal-batch, approximately equal-memory comparison. The latter provides useful evidence of throughput improvements beyond simply increasing batch size.
Includes substantial ablations covering quantization and eviction components, precision assignments, refresh intervals, layer selection, retention levels, and block sizes.
weaknesses: The stated eviction policy does not explain how it satisfies small cache budgets. Retaining at least four tokens from every 128-token segment requires at least 1,024 tokens after 32K generated tokens, excluding the prompt and buffers. Budgets of 64–512 tokens therefore require eventually deleting segments or violating the retention floor, neither of which is specified. This directly affects interpretation of the main compression results.

The evaluation does not adequately isolate the central contribution of thought adaptation. Missing controls include uniform 4-bit quantization combined with the same eviction policy, existing eviction methods combined with comparable quantization, and periodic segment eviction with matched frequency and clustering. Component ablations and attention-recall measurements do not establish that semantic thought categories cause the gains. Related hybrid methods such as Q-Hitter and MiniKV are discussed but not evaluated.

The semantic interpretation of attention sparsity remains insufficiently validated. Illustrative keyword alignments and selected association maps do not establish reliable reasoning/execution/transition classification across models and prompts. There is no quantitative annotation agreement or analysis of whether thresholds calibrated on uncompressed attention remain valid as quantization and eviction change the attention distribution.

Important implementation details are ambiguous. K-means centroids generally are not existing tokens, yet the method retains their 'corresponding' values without specifying representative selection. Per-channel key quantization shares scales across token groups, but arbitrary slot reuse needs an explanation of scale preservation or requantization. Likewise, soft-marked eviction and an unchanged attention kernel leave unclear whether logically evicted entries remain visible until overwritten.

The accuracy evidence lacks uncertainty estimates and essential evaluation details. AIME contains only 30 sampled questions, so several reported differences correspond to roughly one question; rollout counts, decoding settings, and confidence intervals are not adequately documented. LiveCodeBench version and sample selection are also unspecified. 'Near-lossless' is too broad given losses such as approximately five percentage points for QwQ-32B on LiveCodeBench and 7.4 points for MobileLLM on GSM8K.

The headline throughput result uses fixed 32K generation at each method's maximum batch size and compares primarily against R-KV. The equal-batch experiment still changes both eviction policy and memory management, so it does not cleanly isolate the CT kernel. Production-serving gains remain unverified because integration with optimized serving engines is explicitly deferred.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in long-output reasoning: growing KV-cache memory and the overhead of decode-time eviction. Combining adaptive compression with memory-management changes is practically relevant.

The proposed use of attention sparsity to guide segment-level quantization and progressive eviction is an interesting contribution. Counterfactual importance, association analyses, and quantization-sensitivity experiments provide supporting motivation.
Evaluation covers multiple model families and mathematics and coding benchmarks, with extensive component and hyperparameter ablations. Reported accuracy–memory trade-offs are promising.

The systems evaluation includes overlapped-gather baselines, matched-batch experiments, and a vLLM integration. Table 12 reports approximately 1.36× higher throughput than overlapped R-KV at batch size 256, providing concrete evidence beyond maximum-batch comparisons.
weaknesses: The eviction policy has an unresolved budget inconsistency. Sections 4.3 and 6.3 require retaining at least four tokens from every 128-token segment, implying a cache-size lower bound that grows with generation length. At 32K generated tokens, this already requires roughly 1,000 cached tokens, making the evaluated budgets of 64–512 impossible to maintain without violating the retention rule. Neither the text nor pseudocode specifies a fallback when all segments reach the minimum. This directly affects the interpretation of the compression curves.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the benefit of thought adaptation from combining quantization and eviction. Although hybrid predecessors such as Q-Hitter and MiniKV are discussed, they are not evaluated, nor is a straightforward R-KV-plus-matched-quantization baseline. Table 10 shows that numerical format alone materially affects accuracy, further confounding comparisons against integer-quantized baselines. Matched-memory hybrid controls are needed to establish the central contribution.

The semantic interpretation of the sparsity categories remains insufficiently validated. Selected traces and illustrative keywords do not establish reliable correspondence to reasoning, execution, and transition segments across prompts. There is no quantitative annotation agreement or classification evaluation, and no direct assessment of whether thresholds calibrated on uncompressed attention remain reliable after aggressive eviction and quantization. Algorithm 1 also intersects qualifying layers across prompts without explaining how exactly four layers are selected or what happens when the intersection is empty.

Important implementation details are ambiguous. K-means centroids generally are not existing tokens, yet Section 4.3 and Appendix D.4 describe retaining centroid keys and their corresponding original values without specifying representative selection. The text describes classification using sparsity averaged across selected layers, whereas the pseudocode classifies each layer independently. CT also needs clarification on whether soft-evicted entries remain visible to attention before overwrite and how per-channel quantization scales are maintained when slots are reused across groups.

The near-lossless accuracy claim is broader than the evidence supports. Table 1 includes a 4.98-point LiveCodeBench drop for QwQ-32B; Table 8 shows a 7.4-point GSM8K drop; and Table 9 reports 1.9–2.5-point losses. AIME uses only 30 sampled problems, and eight responses per problem do not replace independent problem coverage. No confidence intervals or paired uncertainty estimates establish that smaller reported differences are negligible.

Reproducibility and systems attribution remain incomplete. The manuscript omits exact LiveCodeBench versions and subsets, sampling parameters, checkpoint revisions, and several calibration and clustering settings. The headline 5.8× speedup uses sequential-gather R-KV and different maximum batch sizes; gains against overlapped R-KV in vLLM are substantially smaller. Applying CT to the baseline eviction policy and reporting physical memory including scales, metadata, buffers, and unreclaimed slots would better establish the source and magnitude of the gains.

strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck: KV-cache growth during long reasoning outputs. Combining adaptive compression with efficient memory management is relevant to both reasoning models and inference systems.
The evaluation covers multiple model families, mathematics and coding benchmarks, and numerous component and hyperparameter ablations. Reported accuracy–memory tradeoffs are promising.

Continuous Thinking provides a potentially useful mechanism for reusing evicted cache slots. The iso-batch, approximately iso-compression comparison in Table 2 and the vLLM experiments in Appendix E.12 provide concrete evidence of system-level benefits beyond increased batch capacity.
weaknesses: The stated eviction policy cannot always satisfy its cache budget. Section 4.3 retains at least four tokens from every 128-token segment, implying at least 1,024 retained tokens after 32K generated tokens, even before accounting for recent segments or the prompt. Budgets of 64–512 tokens therefore require violating this minimum or an additional removal/merging rule. Neither the description nor pseudocode specifies such a rule, leaving the actual algorithm underlying the small-budget results unclear.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the central thought-adaptive contribution. Missing controls include periodic segment eviction without thought labels, randomized labels or transition triggers, and a strong eviction baseline combined with the same quantization formats and memory manager. Existing hybrid methods such as Q-Hitter and MiniKV are discussed but not evaluated. Consequently, the gains could partly reflect generic hybrid compression, different number formats, or less frequent eviction rather than reasoning-aware decisions.

The semantic interpretation of attention sparsity remains insufficiently validated. Selected traces and illustrative keywords do not establish reliable identification of reasoning, execution, and transition thoughts across prompts. There is no quantitative agreement with independently annotated segments or analysis showing that calibrated thresholds remain valid after compression changes the attention distribution. The inter-thought association examples also do not distinguish transition-specific effects from ordinary distance-dependent decay.

Important implementation details are unresolved. K-means centroids generally do not correspond to existing tokens, yet Section 4.3 and Appendix D.4 refer to retaining their corresponding values without defining representative-token selection or value aggregation. Arbitrary reuse of slots also interacts with per-channel key quantization using shared scales across 16 tokens; the paper does not explain scale ownership or requantization when a group mixes surviving and newly inserted tokens. These details affect both correctness and overhead.

Near-lossless accuracy is claimed more broadly than the evidence supports. Table 1 includes a roughly five-point LiveCodeBench drop for QwQ-32B, and Table 8 reports a 7.4-point GSM8K drop for MobileLLM. AIME uses only 30 selected problems, and accuracy uncertainty is not reported despite stochastic sampling. The assertion that a 2,048-token budget preserves accuracy across all settings is not accompanied by a comprehensive corresponding result table.

Reproducibility and performance attribution need strengthening. The LiveCodeBench version/date range, sampling parameters, exact checkpoints, calibrated thresholds, and final layer subsets are not specified sufficiently. Algorithm 1 accepts a desired layer count but never enforces it, while the generation pseudocode classifies layers separately rather than implementing the stated selected-layer average. The headline 5.8× throughput gain compares different maximum batch sizes against sequential R-KV; the more controlled vLLM comparison reports approximately 1.35× at batch 256. These are useful gains, but their distinct experimental conditions should constrain the headline claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-output reasoning inference. Combining adaptive quantization, progressive eviction, and memory-slot reuse is a potentially useful algorithm–system contribution.

The evaluation covers several model families and mathematics and coding benchmarks. Component ablations, quantization sensitivity studies, and comparisons at equal batch sizes provide substantial supporting evidence.
The systems results are promising beyond the headline maximum-batch comparison: the vLLM evaluation reports approximately 1.35× higher throughput than overlapped R-KV at batch size 256.
weaknesses: The stated eviction policy cannot always satisfy the evaluated cache budgets. Retaining at least four tokens from every 128-token segment implies a minimum cache size of approximately Lgen/32: 1,024 tokens at 32K generation, before accounting for prompts and buffers. Budgets of 64–512 tokens therefore become infeasible on sufficiently long outputs. Neither Section 4.3 nor the pseudocode explains how this conflict is resolved, making important accuracy–compression results difficult to interpret.

The comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the proposed thought adaptivity from ordinary hybrid compression. The paper discusses Q-Hitter and MiniKV but does not evaluate them, and lacks a strong baseline combining an existing eviction method with the same quantization formats and comparable memory consumption. Table 10 shows that format choice itself materially affects accuracy. Consequently, superiority over separately evaluated eviction-only and quantization-only methods does not establish the claimed source of improvement.

The interpretation of attention sparsity as semantic thought categories is insufficiently validated. Selected traces and illustrative keywords do not establish classification accuracy, boundary accuracy, or stability after compression changes the attention distribution. Useful controls would include shuffled labels, periodic eviction independent of transitions, and alternative sparsity-based policies with identical precision and retention budgets. Changing the number of categories also changes eviction behavior, so that ablation does not isolate the semantic claim.

Important algorithmic details are inconsistent or underspecified. Algorithm 1 intersects eligible layers across all calibration prompts but does not implement its requested four-layer selection or handle an empty intersection. The main text averages sparsity over selected layers, whereas Listing 1 classifies each layer independently. The clustering description alternates between replacing keys with centroids and selecting representative tokens, without specifying which value corresponds to a synthetic centroid.

The near-lossless accuracy claim needs more careful qualification and statistical support. Table 1 includes a 4.98-percentage-point LiveCodeBench decrease for QwQ-32B, and Table 8 shows a 7.4-point GSM8K decrease. AIME contains only 30 sampled problems; eight responses per problem do not replace problem-level uncertainty estimates. Confidence intervals, exact benchmark subsets, sampling parameters, checkpoint revisions, and calibration-overlap checks are missing.

The strongest throughput claim depends on maximum feasible batch sizes and comparison with sequential-gather R-KV; the optimized vLLM improvement is substantially smaller. Although the paper usefully includes these additional comparisons, it does not isolate memory-slot reuse by applying the same memory-management machinery to a competing eviction policy. Memory accounting also needs explicit treatment of quantization scales, block metadata, buffers, and allocated versus logically retained tokens.
